script: My mother called nine one one the night my brother died and hung up after seven seconds, and I did not find that out until nineteen years later, in a records office, on a Tuesday afternoon. But she never told anyone. Not the police, not my father, not me. For nineteen years I thought she had been asleep. That is what all of us thought. That she went to bed at ten, and found him in the morning, and that was the whole of it. I was not even looking for it. I was pulling old records for something else entirely. Insurance. Paperwork. The kind of thing you do at a desk with a number in your hand. And there it was. Eleven fourteen at night. A seven second call from our house line. Terminated by caller. The call that actually brought anyone came at eleven fifty five. It did not come from our house. It came from the neighbour. I sat in that office and did the arithmetic four times, because I did not want it to be right. I drove to her house that weekend. She was doing the crossword. She has done the crossword every morning for forty years, and she did not put the pen down when I said the time out loud. She said, I know. I asked her what she was doing. All that time, in that house, with him upstairs. What were you doing. And she said, I was counting to a thousand. She had called before. Three times in two years, for the same thing, and every time it cost her more than the last, and the last time he had told her that if she ever called anyone again he would not speak to her for the rest of her life. So she sat down on the stairs and she made herself a rule. If he had not made a sound by one thousand, she would call. She said she got to about nine hundred. And then a dog started barking outside and she lost her place. So she started again from one. She has never said that number out loud again. Not once in nineteen years.
